Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = c("p = .113", "p = .113", "p = .657", "p = .482" ), Sentence = c("In secondary analyses, the association of prior cannabis initiation with binge eating onset was significant among women (OR = 2.63, p < .001) but not men (OR = 1.81, p = .113).", "The estimate among men was 1.81 (95% CI [0.87, 3.76], p = .113; Table 4).", "The direct comparison of initiation before age 15 with initiation at age 15 or older gave an odds ratio of 0.90 (95% CI [0.57, 1.42], p = .657; q = .657).", "The age-interaction test did not show clear variation in the association between prior cannabis initiation and binge-eating onset (F with 4 and 147 degrees of freedom, 0.87; p = .482; q = .482)." )), row.names = c(NA, -4L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame" )) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. text.text: Background: Cannabis use and binge eating often co-occur; however, the order and timing of their onset are not well described in population-based samples, limiting our understanding of potential risk pathways between the two behaviors.
Method: We examined the order and timing of onset of these behaviors among 12,314 adults from the Collaborative Psychiatric Epidemiology Surveys.
Cannabis initiation and recurrent binge eating (i.e., binge eating at least twice weekly for 3 months) were dated using ages of onset reported at a single interview.
Survey-weighted survival and discretetime models estimated cumulative probabilities and adjusted odds ratios (ORs) for onset of each behavior after the other.
Results: Among 251 adults reporting both behaviors, cannabis initiation came first for 62.3% (95% CI [52.9, 71.7]) and binge eating came first for 33.2% (95% CI [23.8, 42.5]).
The median interval between behaviors was 4 to 5 years.

Within 10 years of cannabis initiation, 2.6% (95% CI [1.7, 3.6]) had reported binge eating onset; in contrast, within 10 years of binge eating onset, 35.6% (95% CI [24.7, 45.0]) had reported cannabis initiation.

Prior cannabis initiation was associated with higher annual odds of binge eating onset (OR = 2.23, 95% CI [1.46, 3.39], p < .001), and prior binge eating was associated with higher annual odds of cannabis initiation (OR = 1.61, 95% CI [1.07, 2.42], p = .024).

Conclusions: Each behavior was associated with later onset of the other, suggesting a twoway association rather than a single direction of influence.
Thus, clinicians treating either behavior should consider asking about the other.
However, because onset ages were recalled, prospective research is critical to test causal direction.
Binge eating is defined as eating an unusually large amount of food in a discrete period while experiencing a subjective sense of loss of control over eating (American Psychiatric Association, 2013).

text.formatted: When binge eating recurs at least once weekly for 3 months, it is the defining feature of binge eating disorder and a core feature of bulimia nervosa <ref type="bibr">(American Psychiatric Association, 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Binge eating disorder is common in the United States; in the National Comorbidity Survey Replication, up to 2.8% of adults met lifetime criteria for the diagnosis (Hudson et al., 2007).
text.formatted: Binge eating disorder is common in the United States; in the National Comorbidity Survey Replication, up to 2.8% of adults met lifetime criteria for the diagnosis <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Hudson et al., 2007)</ref>.

text.text: In contrast, in the larger and more recent third National Epidemiologic Survey on Alcohol and Related Conditions, lifetime prevalence was 0.85% for binge eating disorder and 0.28% for bulimia nervosa (Udo & Grilo, 2018).
text.formatted: In contrast, in the larger and more recent third National Epidemiologic Survey on Alcohol and Related Conditions, lifetime prevalence was 0.85% for binge eating disorder and 0.28% for bulimia nervosa <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(Udo & Grilo, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Importantly, many adults also report regular binge eating below these diagnostic thresholds (Keski-Rahkonen, 2021), indicating that binge eating spans a spectrum of severity.
text.formatted: Importantly, many adults also report regular binge eating below these diagnostic thresholds <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Keski-Rahkonen, 2021)</ref>, indicating that binge eating spans a spectrum of severity.

text.text: Binge eating disorder and other specified feeding or eating disorders (OSFED) together account for most eating disorder cases and disability worldwide (Santomauro et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Binge eating disorder and other specified feeding or eating disorders (OSFED) together account for most eating disorder cases and disability worldwide <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Santomauro et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: OSFED includes sub-threshold (e.g., lower frequency) presentations of binge eating disorder and bulimia nervosa; as such, the burden of binge eating extends well beyond the full diagnoses.
Binge eating rarely occurs in isolation.
A meta-analysis of prevalence studies documented that substance use disorders commonly co-occur with eating disorders (Bahji et al., 2019).
text.formatted: A meta-analysis of prevalence studies documented that substance use disorders commonly co-occur with eating disorders <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Bahji et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: The order in which these problems emerge also matters for care.

In a Danish register cohort of 20,759 patients with eating disorders and 83,038 matched controls, anorexia nervosa, bulimia nervosa, and unspecified eating disorders were each followed by elevated risk of illicit substance use disorders over the next 10 years (Skøt et al., 2022).
text.formatted: In a Danish register cohort of 20,759 patients with eating disorders and 83,038 matched controls, anorexia nervosa, bulimia nervosa, and unspecified eating disorders were each followed by elevated risk of illicit substance use disorders over the next 10 years <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Skøt et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: This finding indicates that an eating disorder can precede substance use problems and that elevated risk for illicit substance use disorders may then persist for a decade.
Shared biology may also contribute to this clinical overlap.
For example, a recent genome-wide study reported a positive genetic correlation between cannabis initiation and anorexia nervosa with binge eating (Munn-Chernoff et al., 2021).
text.formatted: For example, a recent genome-wide study reported a positive genetic correlation between cannabis initiation and anorexia nervosa with binge eating <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Munn-Chernoff et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Such a correlation suggests that some of the same inherited influences may raise risk for both behaviors.
Cannabis is a particularly plausible contributor to binge eating given its direct effects on appetite.
In a randomized, placebo-controlled trial of 82 adults, vaporized cannabis increased food intake irrespective of dose or gender (Hume et al., 2025).
text.formatted: In a randomized, placebo-controlled trial of 82 adults, vaporized cannabis increased food intake irrespective of dose or gender <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Hume et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Parallel rodent experiments traced this effect to greater reward value of food and greater motivation to obtain it (Hume et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Parallel rodent experiments traced this effect to greater reward value of food and greater motivation to obtain it <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Hume et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: These results identify a potential biological route by which cannabis could amplify the drive for food.

While greater appetite does not by itself amount to binge eating, an increase in food reward offers a credible path from cannabis use to binge eating given that food reward appears to be heightened among individuals who binge eat.

For example, a systematic review of neuroimaging studies found that individuals who binge eat show structural and functional changes in the brain reward system that are linked to greater sensitivity to food (Leenaerts et al., 2022).
text.formatted: For example, a systematic review of neuroimaging studies found that individuals who binge eat show structural and functional changes in the brain reward system that are linked to greater sensitivity to food <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Leenaerts et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Patients with binge eating disorder also showed greater pleasantness and desire to eat in response to food pictures than controls when negative emotions were induced (Arend et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Patients with binge eating disorder also showed greater pleasantness and desire to eat in response to food pictures than controls when negative emotions were induced <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Arend et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Together, these studies suggest that individuals prone to binge eating already respond strongly to food reward; as such, a cannabis-related rise in that reward could matter more for them than for others.
Cross-sectional studies are consistent with this idea but cannot confirm it.
Among 1,568 young adults, 24% of women who used cannabis reported binge eating compared with 13% of women who did not.
No such association appeared among men (Elran-Barak et al., 2025).
text.formatted: No such association appeared among men <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Elran-Barak et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: These results indicate that the two behaviors are linked among young women, and as such sex is an important factor to examine here.
A second study points to a possible pathway.
Among 805 college students who used cannabis, cannabis-related problems were linked with eating pathology through loss-of-control eating (Maynard et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Among 805 college students who used cannabis, cannabis-related problems were linked with eating pathology through loss-of-control eating <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Maynard et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: In other words, loss of control over eating may be the step that connects problematic cannabis use to other disordered eating symptoms.
Cannabis use is also common among individuals already seeking treatment for binge eating.

Among 165 treatment-seeking adults, more than 23% reported cannabis use in the previous 3 months; however, cannabis use was not associated with eating disorder symptoms in that sample (Wilkinson et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Among 165 treatment-seeking adults, more than 23% reported cannabis use in the previous 3 months; however, cannabis use was not associated with eating disorder symptoms in that sample <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(Wilkinson et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: This finding suggests that cannabis use is common among individuals who binge eat but may not mark more severe symptoms.
Thus, its role may be better examined through timing than through severity.
All of the above studies measured both behaviors at a single time point and, as such, cannot establish which behavior came first.
Existing prospective evidence partially addresses this limitation but points in the opposite direction (i.e., from binge eating to later cannabis use).
In a cohort of 16,882 adolescents and young adults, binge eating predicted later initiation of cannabis use (OR = 1.85, 95% CI [1.27, 2.67]; Sonneville et al., 2013).
text.formatted: In a cohort of 16,882 adolescents and young adults, binge eating predicted later initiation of cannabis use (OR = 1.85, 95% CI [1.27, 2.67]; <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">Sonneville et al., 2013)</ref>.

text.text: This result suggests that binge eating may itself raise the likelihood of later trying cannabis.
No studies to date have examined the reverse longitudinal pathway, wherein cannabis use may raise risk for later binge eating.
Taken together, these findings leave the direction of influence unsettled.
Appetite research suggests that cannabis could lead to binge eating, whereas prospective data suggest the reverse.
Further, several underlying mechanisms that may drive cannabis use and binge eating also lead to ambiguous directionality.
For example, emotional distress consistently precedes binge eating (Borm et al., 2025), and depression is associated with past-month cannabis use among US adults (Gorfinkel et al., 2020).
text.formatted: For example, emotional distress consistently precedes binge eating <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Borm et al., 2025)</ref>, and depression is associated with past-month cannabis use among US adults <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Gorfinkel et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Thus, distress alone could generate both behaviors in either order, and shared genetic risk as described above could do the same (Munn-Chernoff et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Thus, distress alone could generate both behaviors in either order, and shared genetic risk as described above could do the same <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Munn-Chernoff et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Given that these accounts predict different orders and timing of onset, describing the actual sequence is a critical first step.
This task has become increasingly urgent as the popularity and legality of cannabis use have grown.
In 2022, daily or near-daily cannabis users outnumbered daily or near-daily drinkers for the first time (Caulkins, 2024).
text.formatted: In 2022, daily or near-daily cannabis users outnumbered daily or near-daily drinkers for the first time <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Caulkins, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: As such, more individuals are exposed to any effect of cannabis on eating than in earlier decades.
Notably, binge eating has also become more common.
In six surveys of Australian adults conducted between 1998 and 2015, the prevalence of binge eating increased over time (Mitchison et al., 2017).
text.formatted: In six surveys of Australian adults conducted between 1998 and 2015, the prevalence of binge eating increased over time <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Mitchison et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Thus, the overlap between the two behaviors may matter for a growing number of individuals.
To address this gap, the current study used the Collaborative Psychiatric Epidemiology Surveys to answer three questions.
First, what was the usual order and interval between cannabis initiation and recurrent binge eating onset among adults who reported both?
Second, how likely was the second behavior to begin within 1, 5, and 10 years after the first?
Third, after adjustment for age, sex, birth cohort, race and ethnicity, and source survey, was the onset of one behavior associated with later onset of the other?
Secondary analyses also examined the role of sex and age at cannabis initiation.
Given that onset dates for both binge eating and cannabis use were retrospectively self-reported at a single interview, this study should be considered descriptive and hypothesis-generating.

Data came from the public-use Collaborative Psychiatric Epidemiology Surveys (CPES), which combine the National Comorbidity Survey Replication, the National Latino and Asian American Study, and the National Survey of American Life (NSAL) (Alegria et al., 2024; Heeringa et al., 2004).

Reported sequence and intervals.
Among participants reporting both behaviors, we classified onset as cannabis first, binge eating first, or the same reported age.
We calculated weighted proportions with 95% confidence intervals.
Within each strictly ordered sequence, the positive difference between onset ages supplied the interval summarized by a weighted median and interquartile range.

We also described onset ages and interval ranges within each sequence.
Elapsed time to the second onset.
We formed two risk sets.
The cannabis-to-bingeeating analysis included participants who had initiated cannabis and either had no recurrent binge eating or reported binge-eating onset at a later age.
The reverse analysis included participants with recurrent binge eating who either had never used cannabis or initiated it at a later age.
Each analysis excluded participants whose second behavior occurred earlier or at the same reported age, and those with no positive observed elapsed time.
Time began at the first behavior.
An event occurred at the second onset, and participants without that onset were censored at age at interview.
These analyses used all available elapsed time without the age-60 cap used in the age-based models below.
We estimated survey-weighted survival functions using the hazard-based Aalen estimator implemented by svykm with standard errors (Lumley).

We report estimates at 1, 5, and 10 years, with unweighted numbers at risk.
Curves were not covariate-adjusted.
Censoring at interview assumes that, within the represented population, remaining observation time is not related to an unobserved second onset in a way that distorts the estimates.
The two curves describe different eligible populations and were not compared as a test of causal direction.
Numbers at risk included participants whose event or censoring time was at least the stated year.
We also reported unweighted event counts and the observed duration from first onset to the second onset or interview.
This duration includes censored observations.
It differs from the interval among participants reporting both behaviors.
Age-based bidirectional models.
We fitted two models using a discrete-time survival framework (Singer & Willett, 1993).
text.formatted: We fitted two models using a discrete-time survival framework <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Singer & Willett, 1993)</ref>.

text.text: Participants contributed one record for each year of age from 5 through the earliest of outcome onset, age at interview, or age 60.
An event indicator identified the outcome-onset year.
The other behavior was a time-varying predictor that became positive only in the year after its reported onset.
Thus, same-age onsets did not contribute as exposed outcome events.
The primary models estimated a common prioronset odds ratio across age.
Separate survey-weighted logistic models used a quasibinomial distribution with a logit link and the adjustment factors described above.
The age spline had boundary knots at 5 and 60, with internal knots at 14, 23, and 35 for the binge-eating model and 12, 21, and 34 for the cannabis model.
Reference categories were male sex, birth cohort 1944 or earlier, Asian or other ancestry, and the National Comorbidity Survey Replication.
The survey design accounted for repeated person-year records within the original sampling clusters.
Exponentiated coefficients are adjusted odds ratios for onset within a year, not Cox hazard ratios.
Regression confidence intervals used the coefficient plus or minus 1.96 standard errors.
Two-sided p values used the survey model degrees of freedom.
Secondary analyses.
The cannabis-to-binge-eating model was repeated separately for women and men, omitting sex from the adjustment set.
A further model replaced prior cannabis initiation with three time-varying categories.
Person-years before cannabis initiation or among never users were the reference, compared with years after initiation at age 15 or older and years after initiation before age 15.
All other covariates and the age spline were unchanged.
In post hoc analyses, we tested a prior-initiation-by-sex interaction in a pooled model with the same covariates and directly compared the two initiation-age coefficients in the categorical model.

Among participants aged at least 30 at interview, we estimated the weighted proportion reporting binge-eating onset by age 30, separately for cannabis initiation before age 18 and no initiation before age 18.
The latter included later initiators and never users.
These unadjusted proportions used logit-transformed confidence intervals.
Because this comparison did not require cannabis initiation to precede binge eating, it was treated as descriptive.
All regression tests were two-sided, with p below .05 considered nominally significant.
Confidence intervals were 95%.
Primary and original secondary p values were not corrected for multiple testing.
As an additional check, we applied the Benjamini-Hochberg correction to the two primary directional tests.
The two new post hoc subgroup comparisons were corrected as a separate family of two, with q below .05 indicating significance after correction (Benjamini & Hochberg, 1995).

We repeated both directional models without the age-60 cap, after excluding all participants who reported both onsets at the same age, and using 2001 instead of 2003 to approximate birth year.

Splines were recalculated in each model.
Other covariates and the one-year exposure lag were unchanged.
Logit models are reported as odds ratios; exponentiated complementary log-log coefficients describe associations on a proportional-hazards scale.

These bounds did not use partial onset information and are not confidence intervals.
In further post hoc checks, we added interactions between prior onset and the four age-spline terms to each directional model.
Joint survey-adjusted Wald F tests assessed age variation.
Benjamini-Hochberg correction was applied to these two tests as a separate exploratory family.

text.text: These checks do not resolve selection arising from unavailable onset ages or unmeasured confounding.
The age-interaction test did not show clear variation in the association between prior cannabis initiation and binge-eating onset (F with 4 and 147 degrees of freedom, 0.87; p = .482; q = .482).
The reverse association varied with age in this diagnostic (F with 4 and 147 degrees of freedom, 4.74; p = .0013; q = .0025).

In this study, we examined the order and timing of cannabis initiation and recurrent binge eating onset in a pooled sample of US adults from three national surveys.
Overall, findings indicate that each behavior was associated with later onset of the other.

After adjustment for age, sex, birth cohort, race and ethnicity, and source survey, prior cannabis initiation was associated with 2.23 times the annual odds of binge eating onset, while prior binge eating was associated with 1.61 times the annual odds of cannabis initiation.
In practical terms, individuals who have begun either behavior have higher odds of beginning the other in a given year than same-aged individuals who have not.
Both associations remained significant after correction for multiple testing and were stable across sensitivity checks.
The descriptive results are consistent with this interpretation.

Specifically, among adults who reported both behaviors with usable onset ages, cannabis came first for 62.3% and binge eating came first for 33.2%, with the second behavior beginning a median of 4 to 5 years after the first.
Taken together, these results describe a two-way association rather than a single fixed sequence.
Importantly, the majority of cannabis-first reports should not be taken as evidence that cannabis drives binge eating.
Cannabis initiation typically occurred in the teen years in these data.
Among adults who reported both behaviors, the weighted median onset age was 17 years for cannabis and 19 years for recurrent binge eating.
Binge eating also typically begins from the late teens to the early twenties (Kessler et al., 2013).
text.formatted: Binge eating also typically begins from the late teens to the early twenties <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Kessler et al., 2013)</ref>.

text.text: As such, the two behaviors share a developmental window.
Given that their onsets cluster within a few years of each other, a small difference in recalled age can decide which behavior appears to come first.
Thus, cannabis would come first in many cases even if the two behaviors were unrelated.
The adjusted models account for this age pattern; as such, the associations they show are not simply a product of cannabis starting earlier in life.
However, the remaining associations are observational and should be interpreted as links rather than causal effects.
The 62.3% cannabis-first estimate also applies only to participants with usable onset ages.
Allowing any ordering for the 116 excluded participants who reported both behaviors gave bounds of 40.2% to 75.7% for the cannabis-first proportion among all 367.
A cannabis-first majority is therefore not established for the broader group.
The onset ages within each sequence offer additional nuance.
When binge eating came first, it began early (unweighted median age 14.5 years) and cannabis initiation followed at a median age of 18 years.
When cannabis came first, cannabis began at a median age of 16 years and binge eating followed at a median age of 22 years.
These medians may indicate two patterns: 1) early-onset binge eating that precedes cannabis initiation and 2) binge eating that emerges in the early twenties after cannabis use has begun.
These patterns may reflect different pathways that future work can separate.
The cumulative probabilities should also be interpreted with care.
Among adults who had begun using cannabis and had not yet reported binge eating, only 2.6% reported recurrent binge eating within 10 years.
In contrast, among adults with recurrent binge eating who had not yet used cannabis, 35.6% reported cannabis initiation within 10 years.
This large gap likely reflects differences in how common each behavior is.
Cannabis initiation was reported by 4,418 participants while recurrent binge eating was reported by only 495, and the two risk sets also differed greatly in size and composition.
As such, the gap says little about which direction of influence is stronger.
The adjusted odds ratios offer a fairer comparison, as they contrast person-years with and without the earlier behavior at the same age.

Those estimates were 2.23 and 1.61, respectively, and their confidence intervals overlapped, which may indicate comparable strengths of association (although we did not formally test this difference).
Thus, the current data do not show that either direction is stronger than the other.
The reverse-direction estimate also should not be assumed to apply equally at every age.
A diagnostic age-interaction test indicated variation across ages for cannabis initiation after binge eating but not for binge eating after cannabis initiation, and older-age estimates were unstable.
Turning first to binge eating as an antecedent, our estimate is similar in size to a prospective estimate from adolescents and young adults (OR = 1.85; Sonneville et al., 2013).
text.formatted: Turning first to binge eating as an antecedent, our estimate is similar in size to a prospective estimate from adolescents and young adults (OR = 1.85; <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">Sonneville et al., 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Notably, agreement across different samples and designs increases confidence that this direction is not specific to a single sample.
This finding is also consistent with evidence of elevated risk for illicit substance use disorders following an eating disorder diagnosis for up to 10 years (Skøt et al., 2022).
text.formatted: This finding is also consistent with evidence of elevated risk for illicit substance use disorders following an eating disorder diagnosis for up to 10 years <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Skøt et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Taken together, these studies suggest that a history of binge eating may be a marker of later cannabis exposure that clinicians can anticipate.
The opposite direction (i.e., cannabis initiation preceding binge eating onset) represents the novel contribution of the current study to the literature.
Earlier evidence for this direction was purely cross-sectional (Elran-Barak et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Earlier evidence for this direction was purely cross-sectional <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Elran-Barak et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Our findings add to that evidence by demonstrating that prior cannabis initiation was associated with later binge eating onset after adjustment for age.
This association was stable across sensitivity analyses.
Several mechanisms could account for this association.
Laboratory work shows that cannabis increases food intake and the reward value of food (Hume et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Laboratory work shows that cannabis increases food intake and the reward value of food <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Hume et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Loss of control over eating may connect cannabis-related problems with eating pathology (Maynard et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Loss of control over eating may connect cannabis-related problems with eating pathology <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Maynard et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Distress may feed both pathways given that it precedes binge eating (Borm et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Distress may feed both pathways given that it precedes binge eating <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Borm et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Shared genetic risk could also contribute (Munn-Chernoff et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Shared genetic risk could also contribute <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Munn-Chernoff et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: These mechanisms are not mutually exclusive, and our models did not include mood or other psychiatric symptoms.
As such, our findings cannot determine which mechanism, if any, is operating on these relationships.
Although the current data cannot identify the operative mechanism, the evidence reviewed above can be integrated into a single reciprocal account that is consistent with our results.
Specifically, shared vulnerability in adolescence (e.g., emotional distress and inherited risk) may raise the likelihood of both behaviors and thus produce both orders of onset.
Distress also heightens the response to food among patients with binge eating disorder (Arend et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Distress also heightens the response to food among patients with binge eating disorder <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Arend et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Once cannabis is initiated, its effect on food reward (Hume et al., 2025) could add to this baseline sensitivity and make loss of control over eating more likely (Maynard et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Once cannabis is initiated, its effect on food reward <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Hume et al., 2025)</ref> could add to this baseline sensitivity and make loss of control over eating more likely <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Maynard et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Once binge eating is established, distress and loss of control could in turn raise the appeal of cannabis given that depression is associated with cannabis use (Gorfinkel et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Once binge eating is established, distress and loss of control could in turn raise the appeal of cannabis given that depression is associated with cannabis use <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Gorfinkel et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Under this account, each behavior raises the odds of the other, which would explain three features of our results: 1) associations in both directions, 2) odds ratios of similar size (2.23 and 1.61), and 3) a gap of several years rather than a fixed sequence.
However, this account remains a hypothesis given that our data contain no measures of the proposed mediators, and future research should empirically evaluate these pathways.
Interestingly, the strength of the cannabis-to-binge-eating association appeared to vary by sex, such that it was larger among women (OR = 2.63) than among men (OR = 1.81).
A post hoc test of the sex interaction was nominally significant but did not meet the corrected significance threshold.
Thus, this contrast should be considered suggestive rather than established.
However, this pattern is consistent with a prior report of an association among young women but not young men (Elran-Barak et al., 2025).
text.formatted: However, this pattern is consistent with a prior report of an association among young women but not young men <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Elran-Barak et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Biological differences alone seem an unlikely explanation given that controlled studies of vaporized cannabis found no systematic sex differences in acute effects (Arkell et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Biological differences alone seem an unlikely explanation given that controlled studies of vaporized cannabis found no systematic sex differences in acute effects <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Arkell et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Other explanations (e.g., differences in why or how women and men use cannabis) should be tested in future research.

Age at initiation also did not meaningfully change this pattern; initiation before age 15 and at age 15 or older were both significantly associated with later binge eating onset, and earlier initiation did not carry a clearly larger association.
A descriptive comparison gave a complementary view.

Among adults aged 30 or older, 4.4% of those who initiated cannabis before age 18 had reported binge eating onset by age 30 compared with 1.6% of those who did not initiate before age 18 (i.e., later initiators and never users).
This comparison was unadjusted and combined participants with different onset sequences.
It therefore cannot show that early initiation caused later binge eating.
These findings have important clinical implications.
Cannabis use is already common among adults seeking treatment for binge eating.
In one clinical sample, more than 23% reported recent use (Wilkinson et al., 2024).
text.formatted: In one clinical sample, more than 23% reported recent use <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(Wilkinson et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Our estimate that 35.6% of adults with recurrent binge eating who had not yet used cannabis initiated within 10 years indicates that cannabis initiation after binge eating onset is common.
Thus, clinicians who treat binge eating should consider asking about cannabis use at intake and again over time.
The reverse is also true.

Given that cannabis came first for most adults with usable onset ages who reported both behaviors (although this majority is not established for the broader group), clinicians who treat cannabis use should consider asking about binge eating.
Loss of control over eating may be a useful focus for those questions (Maynard et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Loss of control over eating may be a useful focus for those questions <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Maynard et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: This need is likely growing given that frequent cannabis use is now more common than when these surveys were conducted (Caulkins, 2024).
text.formatted: This need is likely growing given that frequent cannabis use is now more common than when these surveys were conducted <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Caulkins, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Several directions for future research follow from these findings.

First, prospective cohorts that repeatedly assess cannabis use and binge eating are critical for establishing order without relying on recall, which is the main limitation of the sequence estimates reported here.
Second, future research should measure the frequency, dose, and potency of cannabis use to determine whether heavier or more potent use carries greater risk.

Third, repeated sampling of mood, cannabis use, and eating in daily life (e.g., via ecological momentary assessment) could test whether cannabis use changes the likelihood of loss-ofcontrol eating on the same day.
This approach has already been used to study distress and binge eating (Borm et al., 2025).
text.formatted: This approach has already been used to study distress and binge eating <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Borm et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Fourth, models that add education, childhood adversity, other substance use, and psychiatric history with their ages of onset are needed to test whether the associations persist after adjustment.
Fifth, replication of the sex difference in larger cohorts that use the once-weekly DSM-5 threshold is needed to determine whether the pattern among women is robust and generalizable.
Sixth, cohorts with complete onsetage data are needed to address the selection that arises when onset ages are missing.
The current study has several notable strengths.
First, the data come from probability samples that include several racial and ethnic groups.
Second, survey weights and design variables allow the estimates to approximate the population rather than only the sample.
However, it remains unconfirmed whether the long-form weight fully accounts for selection into the eating-disorder module.
Third, censoring methods retained adults who had not yet reported the second behavior, which avoided discarding the many adults who had not yet developed it.
Fourth, each direction was analyzed separately so that neither depended on the other.
Finally, the primary associations remained significant after correction for multiple testing and were stable across sensitivity checks.
Findings from the current study should be interpreted in light of several limitations.
First, onset ages were retrospectively recalled by adults at a single interview.
Recall of past psychiatric history is imperfect and may differ by age and by how severe or recurrent the problem was (Simon & VonKorff, 1995).
text.formatted: Recall of past psychiatric history is imperfect and may differ by age and by how severe or recurrent the problem was <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Simon & VonKorff, 1995)</ref>.

text.text: As such, misdated onsets could reverse some sequences.
Ages were reported in whole years and 17 participants reported the same age for both behaviors, so those cases could not be ordered.
Second, few participants reported both behaviors (n = 251).
Sequence and interval estimates are imprecise, particularly for the binge-eating-first group (n = 82).
Third, binge eating was defined by two interview items without a requirement for loss of control or distress.
Further, the twice-weekly threshold is stricter than the once-weekly DSM-5 threshold (American Psychiatric Association, 2013).
Accordingly, adults whose binge eating was less frequent were classified as not having recurrent binge eating, and the measure does not identify DSM-5 consistent binge eating disorder.
Likewise, cannabis initiation does not indicate regular use or DSM-5 consistent cannabis use disorder.
The findings apply to the onset of these behaviors rather than to clinical diagnoses.
Fourth, the models did not adjust for education, tobacco use, alcohol use, psychiatric symptoms, or childhood adversity.
Residual confounding is likely, and thus the associations should not be interpreted as causal.
Education and childhood adversity are plausible confounders that should be included in future models.
Tobacco use, alcohol use, and psychiatric symptoms are also plausible confounders; however, they may begin after cannabis use or binge eating or lie on the pathway between them.
Adjusting for these variables would thus require their ages of onset and a time-varying design.
Fifth, survival curves were not adjusted for covariates and the yearly odds ratios are not hazard ratios, both of which limit direct comparison with studies that report hazard ratios.
Sixth, primary and original secondary tests were not corrected for multiple testing.
The two primary directional tests remained significant after Benjamini-Hochberg correction.
However, the post hoc analyses were not prespecified.
Isolated p-values near .05 should therefore be interpreted with caution.
Seventh, onset ages were unusable for 116 of the 367 participants who reported both behaviors (31.6%), and exclusion was more common among participants reporting recurrent binge eating (32.3%).
The sequence estimates therefore describe only participants with usable onset ages, and conservative bounds for the full group (40.2% to 75.7% cannabis first) were wide.
Approximate onset-age fields were unavailable and could not reduce this loss.
Eighth, the NSAL White sample was not administered the substanceuse or eating-disorder sections.
The pooled sample therefore does not represent all US adults.
It also remains unconfirmed whether the long-form weight accounts for selection into the eating-disorder module.
Ninth, the association between prior binge eating and cannabis initiation varied with age (p = .0013), and older-age estimates were unstable.
The overall odds ratio of 1.61 should therefore not be assumed to apply at every age.
Finally, the surveys were conducted in 2001 to 2003.
Cannabis use has become more frequent since then (Caulkins, 2024).
text.formatted: Cannabis use has become more frequent since then <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Caulkins, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Thus, the timing and strength of the associations may differ in current cohorts.
In US adults, cannabis initiation and recurrent binge eating were each associated with later onset of the other.
Cannabis most often came first among adults who reported both behaviors with usable onset ages, while binge eating came first for about one third.
Taken together, these findings are more consistent with a two-way association than a single direction of influence.
Thus, asking about each behavior in the care of the other is a reasonable response, and prospective research is needed to clarify causal direction.
